items.title: If you can't test, add a holding dose
items.because: If you can't test today, 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine raises free chlorine by about 1.5 ppm. That is a holding dose, not a shock: 2 ppm is below what you would swim in, so it cannot over-chlorinate the pool, and it buys a day without pretending to know what the level actually is. Test before adding any more than this.
items.why: ORP is 531 mV and free chlorine isn't measured, so you don't know if the pool is holding sanitizer. If you can't test, this holding dose brings free chlorine up to a level that keeps the water protected without pretending to know the real number. It is not a shock, and it can't over-chlorinate the pool.
items.how: Only do this if you can't test today. Make sure the pump is running, then pour the 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine slowly around the deep end, standing back so it doesn't splash you or the deck. Keep the pump running afterward, and don't put acid or any other chemical in the same bucket or in the water at the same time.

items.title: Test free chlorine today
items.because: ORP is 531 mV, well under the 550 mV mark where the water may genuinely not be sanitising. Free chlorine isn't measured -- the ICO can't read it -- so nobody knows whether that is a real chlorine shortage or just the proxy sagging. Salt is out of band, which depresses ORP on its own, so this may resolve once it is fixed. It is still worth a strip test today rather than assuming.
items.why: ORP is 531 mV, under the 600 mV floor. It is also under the 550 mV mark where the water may not be sanitizing. Free chlorine isn't measured, so you can't tell whether that is a real chlorine shortage or the low salt dragging ORP down. A strip test today settles it.
items.how: Dip a strip into water taken from elbow depth, away from the return jets, and read it right away against the chart. Write the free chlorine number down so the next dose is based on a measurement.

items.title: Add salt
items.because: Salt is 2,352 ppm, below the 2800-3200 ppm the cell needs. A cell run under its salt band makes less chlorine and wears out faster.
items.why: Salt is 2,352 ppm against a 2,800–3,200 band. The cell makes less chlorine below that band and wears out faster, which is a big part of why ORP is sitting at 531 mV. Adding salt is the fix that helps everything else on the list.
items.how: Run the pump, then predissolve the salt in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water. Pour it in slowly around the deep end so no granules sit on the vinyl liner. If any dry salt lands on the floor, brush it toward the main drain until it's gone, and keep the pump running afterward.

dose.label: 90 lb of salt (about 2.25 of a 40 lb bag)

items.title: Leave the cell alone for now
items.because: ORP is 531 mV, under the at least 600 mV floor -- but Salt is out of band too, and ORP sits downstream of all of it. Fix that first, give the water a full day to circulate, then re-read. Turning the cell up now just means running it harder against the same problem.
items.why: ORP is 531 mV against a 600 floor, but salt is out of band too, and ORP depends on it. Turning the cell up now would just run it harder against the same low-salt problem. Fix the salt first, give the water a full day to circulate, then read ORP again.
items.how: Don't change anything today. Leave the cell setting where it is, and re-check ORP tomorrow after the salt has had time to mix in.

items.title: The cell is already flat out
items.because: The cell is at 100% (from config.json), running 24 hours a day, so there is no headroom left to ask for -- this is not a setting you can turn up. Salt is out of band, and each of those starves the cell in its own way: low salt gives it less to work with, high pH wastes the chlorine it makes, low CYA lets the sun burn it off. Fix those and the same cell will produce more.
items.why: The cell is at 100% and the pump runs 24 hours a day, so there is nothing left to turn up. Low salt gives the cell less to work with, so it can't make the chlorine you need even flat out. Once the salt is back in band, the same cell should produce more.
items.how: Leave the cell at 100% and don't try to push it further. The salt addition above is what will make this cell more effective.

items.title: Leave the pump schedule alone for now
items.because: The pump is running 24 hours a day, which is a lot -- but on a saltwater pool the pump schedule is the chlorine schedule, because the cell only makes chlorine while water is going through it. With ORP at 531 mV, cutting hours would cut production exactly when you need it. Get ORP comfortably over 600 with the cell below full, and that is the moment to start trimming hours and watching what happens.
items.why: The pump runs 24 hours a day, which is a lot, but on a saltwater pool the pump schedule is the chlorine schedule because the cell only works while water flows through it. With ORP at 531 mV, cutting hours would cut chlorine production when you need it most. Trim hours only once ORP is comfortably over 600 with the cell below full.
items.how: Leave the timer as it is. Come back to it after the salt is up and ORP has recovered.

items.title: Test borates
items.because: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and haven't been tested. The target is 50 ppm; a strip test once a season is enough to know where you are.
items.why: Borates weren't measured and aren't on the ICO panel, so you don't know where they stand against the 50 ppm target. A strip test once a season is enough to know.
items.how: Use a borate test strip or kit on a water sample from elbow depth, and follow the timing on the package. Write the result down. This is low priority, so do it after the chlorine test and the salt.

safety_rules: NEVER pour undiluted acid into the skimmer. Acid down the skimmer runs neat through the pump, heater and salt cell and eats them. Dilute it and pour it slowly around the deep end with the pump running.

NEVER put shock and acid in the same session without at least 4 hours between them, and say the gap out loud in the instructions. Both move pH hard in opposite directions, and back to back you cannot tell what the water actually did.
ALWAYS predissolve dry chemicals in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water before they go in. Undissolved granules sitting on a vinyl liner bleach and weaken it.
NEVER put chlorine and acid in the same bucket, in either order. That combination produces chlorine gas.
ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid -- pouring water into acid can boil and spit it back at you.
The pump must be RUNNING before anything goes in, and keep running afterwards, so a dose disperses instead of sitting in one corner.
headline: Salt is low and ORP is soft: test chlorine, then add salt
summary: The reading is from this morning. Salt is 2,352 against a 2,800–3,200 band and ORP is 531 mV against a 600 floor. Free chlorine, CYA, TA and borates weren't measured. Salt is the root problem, so start there and re-read once it has circulated.
